pages.title: What this unit is about
pages.body:
> 💻 **Strand 1 — Introduction To Computing**
Sub-strand 3: Health and Safety in the Use of ICT Tools

In Basic 7 you learnt to set up a safe workstation. This unit builds healthy habits for long periods of computer work and shows you how to reduce risks from sound, light and electricity.

pages.title: Content standard and lessons
pages.body:
> 🎯 **Content standard**
- **B8.1.3.1** Demonstrate how to apply health and safety measures in using ICT tools.

> 🧭 **What you will be able to do**
- **B8.1.3.1.1** Discuss health issues at workstations.

> 🗺️ **Lessons in this unit**

**Core competencies developed:** Personal Development and Leadership (PL5.6), Digital Literacy (DL5.3).

pages.title: Health Issues at Workstations
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B8.1.3.1.1
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- explain the importance of regular breaks;
- adopt good posture at the computer;
- use document holders correctly.
## Taking regular breaks
Working continuously at a computer strains the eyes, back, neck and wrists. Health experts recommend **short, frequent breaks**: at least **5–10 minutes every hour** of bulk work (typing, data entry), during which you stand, stretch, walk and rest your eyes. Short frequent breaks are better than one long break.
| **Simple desk exercises (do each for 10–20 seconds)** |  |
|---|---|
| Neck | Slowly tilt your head to each side and forward |
| Shoulders | Roll your shoulders backwards and forwards |
| Wrists and fingers | Gently stretch your fingers apart; rotate your wrists |
| Eyes | 20-20-20 rule; blink slowly ten times |
| Back | Stand, place hands on hips and gently lean back |
## Good posture
- Sit right back in the chair with your lower back supported.
- Keep your head upright, not bent forward; the top of the screen should be at or slightly below eye level.
- Shoulders relaxed; elbows close to the body at about 90°; wrists straight.
- Thighs roughly parallel to the floor; feet flat on the floor or a footrest.
- Hold phones and tablets nearer to eye level instead of bending your neck.

pages.title: Document holders
pages.body:
## Document holders
A **document holder** is a stand that holds papers upright next to (or between) the keyboard and screen at about the same height and distance as the screen. It stops you from repeatedly bending your neck down to read paperwork while typing, reducing neck and eye strain.
> 🧪 **Activity**
Role-play: one learner types a page from a textbook placed flat on the desk while another observes their neck. Repeat with the book propped upright beside the screen. Discuss the difference.

pages.title: Safety Measures for Risk Reduction
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B8.1.3.1.2
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- demonstrate safe listening volumes;
- use screen filters and protective eyewear appropriately;
- avoid overloading electrical sockets.
## Safe listening
Loud sound damages tiny hair cells in the inner ear, and the damage is permanent. The World Health Organization advises safe listening: keep personal audio below about **60% of maximum volume**, limit listening time, use **noise-cancelling** headphones so you don’t need to turn the volume up, and take listening breaks. Most phones can warn you when the volume is too high (headphone safety settings).
## Controlling the light reaching your eyes
- **Anti-glare screen protectors and filters** reduce reflections from windows and lights.
- **Spectacles** prescribed by an optician correct vision problems; anti-reflective lenses reduce glare.
- Use **Night light** (Windows) or **Night mode** on phones in the evening to reduce blue light and help sleep.
- Adjust screen **brightness** to match the room and increase text size if you squint.
## Electrical safety: not overloading sockets
Plugging too many devices into one socket with **plug adapters** (block or “cube” adapters stacked together) can draw more current than the socket is rated for, causing overheating and fire.

pages.title: Safety Measures for Risk Reduction (continued)
pages.body:
| **Do** | **Do not** |
|---|---|
| Use a good-quality **trailing multi-socket extension** with a fuse and surge protection | Stack adapters into one wall socket ("daisy-chaining") |
| Check the total power (watts) of devices against the extension’s rating | Plug one extension into another extension |
| Uncoil cable reels fully before use | Use damaged or hot plugs and extensions |
| Switch off and unplug devices that are not in use | Hide extensions under carpets or mats where heat builds up |
